newsitem.title: USA: GM Oklahoma strike deadline draws closer.
newsitem.headline: GM Oklahoma strike deadline draws closer.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and the autoworkers union edged closer to a midnight strike deadline Friday at the automaker's Oklahoma City car plant, where a walkout would cut off supplies of two key new car models.
About 3,500 members of United Auto Workers Local 1999 were set to strike at 11:59 p.m. local time unless negotiators reached a tentative agreement on a new local labor contract.

The plant is the main production source for GM's new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-size sedans. A strike could deprive GM dealers of the cars in the midst of the automaker's multimillion-dollar national advertising launch for them.
The Malibu and Cutlass, developed under the code-name "P-90" are a cornerstone of GM's efforts to regain market share in the U.S. intermediate car segment, which it once dominated.
GM this week reported stronger-than-expected March U.S. sales of the Malibu, which increased to 12,260 cars from 5,800 in February.

The main sticking point in the negotiations, as in most recent GM labor disputes, is jobs. The union has said it wants GM to hire about 500 new workers to help restore jobs lost to retirements in recent months.
The union contends that its members are being forced to endure an increased workload that is resulting in higher numbers of repetitive trauma injuries.

GM has said the plant needs fewer workers to build the new cars than it needed to build previous models, including the Buick Century and Oldsmobile Ciera. The Malibu and Cutlass are designed with far fewer parts and are easier to build.
Negotiators have worked late into the evening many nights this week and union officials have reported some progress.
"We're still hopeful that we can get it resolved before the deadline," said GM spokesman Charles Licari. He declined to elaborate on the discussions.

The Oklahoma City plant, which has never had a strike in its 18-year history, recently launched production of the all-new Cutlass and Malibu and is up to about 80 percent of its full production capacity.
A second plant, in Wilmington, Del., just began production of Malibus about two weeks ago, but is much further behind on its launch curve.

GM last week settled a nearly two-week strike at its Fort Wayne, Ind., pickup truck plant in a deal that calls for the company to add 276 new workers to the factory's payroll. Most of the workers are expected to be transferred from other GM facilities that have excess workers.

Union sources say there are several other GM plants that have asked UAW headquarters for permission to strike because of slow progress in local negotiations, including a GM transmission plant in Warren, Mich., a foundry in Saginaw, Mich., and another pickup truck assembly plant in Pontiac, Mich.
